headline: Upheld $1,000 fine and three-day tobacco permit suspension for Olympic Wine and Spirits on Grafton Street.
summary: The meeting covered a tobacco violation hearing, a communicable disease update, a kratom overview, Community HealthLink, homelessness efforts, Temporary Protected Status, and the Civilian Review Board. The board voted to uphold the tobacco violation's fine and three-day suspension after the retailer asked for a warning instead. The final vote was 4-0 after Michael Perotto was allowed to vote.

WORCESTER BOARD OF HEALTH MEETING 
Meeting Minutes 
September 30, 2026 
25 MEADE STREET, ROOM 109 1ST FLOOR. WORCESTER, MA 
 
 
Welcome 
 
Board Members Present:  
Chair-Frances Anthes, Dr. Patrick Lowe  
 
Board Members Virtual 
Michael Perotto, Joseph Kahoro 
 
Staff Present:  
Alex Arriaga, HHS A ssistant Commissioner; Jennifer Bradford, Medical Director, HHS; Nick 
Antanavica, Commissioner of Inspectional Services ; Kyle OConnor, Tobacco Prevention 
Specialist. 
 
Staff Virtual:  
Seema Dixit, HHS Commissioner; Desiree Sutton, Business Manager ; Altagracia Soto, Public 
Health Prevention Specialist DPH; Brenda Wright, Principal Clerk;  
 
1. Call to Order 
Chair Frances Anthes called the meeting to order at 6:30pm. 
2. Welcome and Introductions 
Board members introduced themselves: Patrick Lowe, Joseph Kahoro, and Chair Frances Anthes. 
Attendees present and virtual were also asked to introduce themselves 
3. Announcements 
i. The Chair announced that there were still ongoing technical issues streaming on the Teams 
platform, and online participants were asked to enable closed captions to assist in their 
virtual experience.  
ii. The Chair announced that the City Council Standing Committee on Public Health and 
Human Services invited members of the Board to participate in its August 24 meeting to 
discuss youth exposure to tobacco, particularly vaping, following topics raised during the 
Board’s public hearing. 
 
Dr. Patrick Lowe and the Chair, Frances Anthes attended the meeting. Dr. Lowe reported that the 
discussion focused on youth vaping and potential opportunities to mitigate and reduce its impact 
on the city. He said the importance of cross-departmental and citywide collaboration in addressing
youth vaping, extends beyond the Board’s regulatory and enforcement authority. He said currently, 
no formal initiatives were announce d; however, discussions with the City Council, community 
members, and other City departments are expected to continue. 
 
4. Minutes of last meeting 
The Chair requested approval of the minutes from the September 18 meeting. 
 
Patrick Lowe made a motion  to approve the September 18 BOH minutes which was approved 
unanimously by roll call vote, with Joseph Kahoro voting yes, Patrick Lowe - yes, and Frances 
Anthes-yes. 
 
5. Tobacco Retailer Hearing  
Kyle O’Connor, Tobacco Prevention Specialist, presented a violation involving Olympic Wine 
and Spirits, located at 345 Grafton Street, Worcester, for the sale of flavored cigars to a youth 
during a compliance inspection. The retailer failed to properly ver ify the purchaser’s age and 
identification, in violation of the City’s tobacco regulations. 
The Board was informed that this was the retailer’s first violation within the applicable 36-month 
period. Kyle recommended a $1,000 fine and a three -day suspension of the tobacco sales permit, 
in accordance with the City’s regulations. 
The violation occurred on July 24, and the retailer was notified of the hearing scheduled for 
September 30, providing an opportunity to appear before the Board and respond to the violation 
before the Board considered the recommended enforcement action. 
Retailers Response 
Mr. William Krisity, the retailer, provided an explanation of the transaction and accepted 
responsibility for the violation. He described the incident as an isolated employee error that did 
not reflect the store’s normal business practices. He explained that the employee was distracted by 
another matter during the transaction, recognized her mistake, and did not intentionally sell 
tobacco products to an underage customer. 
Mr. Krisity noted that tobacco products account for less than one percent of the store’s total sales 
and are offered primarily as a convenience to customers. He stated that the store carries a limited 
selection of basic tobacco products and has held its tobacco licen se for 17 years, during which it 
has sought to operate responsibly and comply with applicable requirements. 
He expressed concern that the proposed enforcement action was disproportionate to the 
circumstances, arguing that an inadvertent employee error should be distinguished from intentional 
or repeated violations. He also questioned whether the penalties were e quitable when compared 
with those imposed for other serious violations, including the sale of illegal or prohibited products 
to younger customers. Additionally, he raised concerns about the differences between state and 
local requirements and whether the c urrent enforcement approach adequately accounted for the 
circumstances faced by retailers.
Mr. Krisity acknowledged the seriousness of tobacco violations but argued that a three -day 
suspension could place the business at a disadvantage and potentially direct customers to other 
retailers. He respectfully requested that the Board reduce the proposed suspension to a warning. 
Board’s Discussion and response 
The Chair explained that the intent of the Board of Health’s new tobacco regulations was to 
establish clear and strict requirements for addressing individuals and establishments that are 
violators. She noted that, while enforcement is an important component of the regulations, 
education and outreach are also necessary to ensure that tobacco retailers understand the new 
requirements and how they apply to their businesses. 
The Chair stated that Kyle is currently developing an educational process to support 
implementation of the new regulations. She acknowledged that simply posting or distributing new 
regulations does not always ensure that everyone has reviewed or fully understands them. As part 
of the educational process, Kyle will conduct visits with tobacco retailers to provide information, 
clarify the requirements, and help ensure compliance. The Chair indicated that these visits are 
expected to begin soon. 
Patrick Lowe 
Dr. Lowe  thanked the speaker for attending the hearing and expressed well wishes for his 
continued recovery. He clarified that the tobacco regulations adopted over the summer did not 
change the legal age of sale and did not create new financial or suspension penalties that were not 
already in place. He noted that the violation discussed at the hearing would have constituted a 
violation both before and after the adoption of the new regulations. 
Dr. Lowe emphasized that education and outreach are important components of the regulations 
and clarified that the Board’s intent was not to impose unnecessarily severe consequences for a 
first violation, jeopardize a business owner’s livelihood, or encour age the termination of an 
employee over a single incident. He reiterated that the primary goals are to promote education, 
compliance, and proper implementation of the regulations. 
He also acknowledged concerns raised regarding practices of other tobacco retailers and 
encouraged the speaker and other business owners to share information about potential violations 
or practices that may not be readily visible to City staff. He stated that staff and the Board welcome 
additional feedback and information regarding such concerns and could consider whether further 
actions or measures may be appropriate in the future. 
Joseph Kahoro 
Joseph echoed the remarks made by his fellow Board members; he expressed sympathy regarding 
the difficulties the speaker had experienced and reiterated that the primary purpose of the 
regulations is to establish clear guidelines and requirements. He emphasized that the regulations 
were not intended to create undue h ardship and expressed confidence that the concerns raised 
would be addressed and resolved.
The Chair acknowledged that the Board’s new tobacco regulations were controversial in several 
respects during the development and adoption process. She stated that the Board has asked staff to 
closely monitor the implementation of the regulations and to pr ovide timely feedback regarding 
their impact. 
She thanked the speaker for attending the hearing and providing feedback and encouraged him to 
continue communicating with Kyle regarding his concerns and observations. She emphasized that 
the Board intends to closely monitor the implementation of the regulations and their effects on the 
community.  
Board Action 
The Chair called for a motion on t he recommendation from staff that the fine for a first violation 
as outlined in the regulations (a $1,000 fine and a 3 -day suspension of the tobacco sales permit ), 
be upheld. 
Patrick Lowe made a motion to uphold th e violations as reported. The votes were recorded as 
follows: 
Patrick Lowe – yes 
Joseph Kahoro – Yes 
Frances Anthes – yes, carried unanimously. 
 
6. Nursing and Communicable Disease Update:  
Presented by Dr. Jennifer Bradford, HHS Medical Director. 
• The Board received a communicable disease update, including a discussion of recent 
COVID-19 activity. The update noted an increase in COVID -19 cases between July and 
August, with current activity described as moderate. 
• The Board also received an update on the work of the Division of Public Health nurses in 
the community. Nurses continue to conduct vaccination clinics and provide vaccinations 
to community members. 
• The importance of providing accessible vaccination services to the community was 
emphasized, particularly in helping to prevent severe illness. The Board expressed 
appreciation for the nurses' continued efforts to provide vaccination services and outreach 
in the community. 
The presentation can be accessed online at www.worcesterma.gov/public-health 
 
7. Kratom Products Overview and Temporary Ban 
Presenters: Dr. Jennifer Bradford, HHS Medical Director , and Nick Antanavica, ISD 
Commissioner.  
 
The presentation provided an overview of kratom, its potential health risks, and public health 
measures implemented to protect the public. Dr. Bradford provided historical context, noting that 
kratom has been used for centuries in traditional medicine to address various health concerns. She 
discussed growing concerns regarding its health effects and its use by individuals seeking to 
manage withdrawal symptoms.
Dr. Bradford explained that kratom products are sometimes marketed as alternatives to 
medications and are available over the counter. However, their ingredients and concentrations 
may vary significantly, potentially resulting in inconsistent effects and ad verse health outcomes 
among consumers. 
 
Dr. Bradford discussed potential adverse effects associated with kratom use, including withdrawal 
symptoms, nausea, and dizziness.  
 
▪ Potential Risks and Interactions 
Concerns were raised regarding the use of kratom in combination with other substances, including 
opioids, benzodiazepines, and alcohol. Dr. Bradford explained that combining kratom with these 
substances may increase the risk of serious adverse effects, inc luding respiratory depression and 
overdose. She also noted that kratom may interact with medications used to treat other health 
conditions. 
The potential risks were described as particularly concerning for individuals with underlying heart 
or respiratory conditions and those taking multiple medications. Dr. Bradford emphasized the 
importance of raising awareness about kratom use, potential dru g interactions, and the risks 
associated with combining kratom with other substances. Reported adverse effects may include 
withdrawal symptoms, psychosis, delusional thinking, itching, seizures, and hallucinations. 
▪ Federal Action and Public Health Considerations 
Dr. Bradford emphasized the risk of overdose associated with kratom use, particularly when 
combined with other substances, and noted the need for further research into its health effects and 
community impact. She reviewed the DEA’s temporary federal order, effective August 2026 for 
up to one year, restricting three synthetic kratom -related substances . These are Mitragynine 
Pseudoindoxyl, Dihydro-7-hydroxymitragynine (also known as MGM -15) and Dihydro-7-
hydroxymitragynine (also known as MGM-15). She also referenced Massachusetts Department of 
Public Health guidance and noted that kratom had not previously been subject to specific local 
regulation. 
▪ Treatment 
Dr. Bradford discussed how kratom restrictions may affect individuals who have developed a 
dependence on the substance and emphasized the need for appropriate support and treatment 
resources for the public and healthcare providers. She also highlighted ove rdose prevention 
resources, including Narcan (naloxone), which is available without a prescription. 
 
▪ Enforcement and regulatory considerations.  
The Chair asked how the federal action relates to the City’s regulations. Dr. Bradford clarified that 
the federal action targets certain synthetic kratom substances, while Worcester’s regulation covers 
both synthetic and naturally occurring kratom products . Nick noted that kratom is sold over the 
counter in various forms, including powders, capsules, and beverages, at smoke shops, gas stations, 
and other retail locations.
▪ Implementation and Enforcement 
Nick Antanavica, ISD Commissioner, explained that the Division worked with state partners to 
quickly notify food and tobacco license holders of the new requirements. Follow -up inspections 
found that most establishments notified had removed prohibited products, while others were given 
approximately one week to comply. He reported limited resistance from retailers. 
The Division also provided guidance on handling prohibited products, including storage, transfer 
to another state where permitted, or surrender to local law enforcement. No products had been 
reported received by local police at the time of the presentation. 
The Division will continue monitoring compliance, with potential enforcement actions, including 
fines, for violations identified after the compliance period. 
Board Discussions 
Dr. Lowe asked how the city addresses unlicensed tobacco sales outside the Board’s established 
licensing and enforcement structure. The commissioner  explained that the Department meets 
weekly with the Licensing Commission and a Police Department representative to coordinate 
concerns involving licensed and unlicensed establishments. 
 
Dr. Lowe emphasized the need for interdepartmental coordination to ensure prohibited products 
are removed. Nick reported that several establishments had returned products, including one large 
retailer that received approximately 1,500 cases shortly before the anno uncement and was 
arranging their return. Dr. Lowe commended the federal, state, and local response and highlighted 
the public health risks associated with unregulated products, including overdose and withdrawal. 
 
Dr. Bradford stressed the importance of public education in terms of  the potential dangers of 
unregulated products, noting that over -the-counter availability may lead consumers to assume 
they are safe. 
 
Fran also asked how the city identifies and addresses unlicensed establishments, and how existing 
regulatory functions could support enforcement efforts.  Nick explained that the Department is 
conducting outreach to gas stations, smoke shops, convenience stores, and other establishments, 
regardless of whether they hold a tobacco license. He noted that the product is prohibited and 
cannot be kept on shelves, and that establishments are being advised to remove it. He further 
stated that enforcement has progressed to the punitive stage when violations are identified and 
encouraged establishments with questions to contact DPH or Inspectional Services for assistance 
with compliance. 
 
The chair thanked Dr. Bradford and Commissioner Antanavica for an informative presentation. 
The presentation can be accessed online at www.worcesterma.gov/public-health 
 
8. Community HealthLink Update- Seema Dixit, HHS Commissioner  
The Commissioner provided an update on Community Health Link (CHL), noting that community 
listening sessions had been held and that CHL had met with other behavioral health providers to
discuss the transition plan. Detoxification beds had transitioned to other levels of care, and 
remaining services had been assumed by other agencies. She will continue updating the Board as 
information becomes available. 
Fran asked whether patients might experience gaps in care or be unaware of where to access 
services during the transition. Seema responded that it was too early to assess the impact but 
anticipated receiving additional feedback on patient experiences and access challenges within the 
next 30 to 60 days. The Chair thanked her for the update. 
9. City’s Efforts on Un -Housed Population  - Seema Dixit, HHS Commissioner 
and Alex Arriaga, Assistant Commissioner, HHS 
The Board requested an update on the City Council’s recent discussion of the City’s homelessness 
strategic framework, “Disrupting the Cycle.” Seema provided an overview of the framework, 
noting that the Health and Human Services team has worked with commun ity partners through a 
monthly homelessness steering committee for approximately 15 –17 months to review data, 
identify service needs, and improve coordination. 
The framework emphasizes data sharing, coordination among service providers, and training for 
outreach staff to ensure consistent engagement and connections to appropriate services. Seema 
also discussed a proposed encampment ordinance that would involve id entifying encampments, 
conducting repeated outreach, providing notice, and connecting individuals with available services 
before removal to address public health and safety concerns. 
She added that the City  is developing a centralized database to track service utilization, identify 
gaps, and improve coordination among providers. The framework aims to strengthen service 
delivery and improve outcomes for individuals experiencing homelessness. 
Board’s response 
Joseph Kahoro acknowledged the sensitivity of homelessness and commended the City’s efforts 
to streamline services and address the issue. 
 
Fran asked about the number of individuals experiencing homelessness in Worcester and available 
shelter capacity. Seema explained that estimates vary due to the changing population and methods 
of data collection. She reported approximately 60 –65 individual s experiencing chronic 
homelessness, with an estimated 200–250 individuals experiencing homelessness on a given day. 
She noted that the City has approximately 200 shelter beds, but individuals require different levels 
of support, including shelter, clinical care, detoxification, addiction services, and specialized 
housing. 
 
Seema described the City’s efforts to map available resources and use outreach and encampment 
assessments to identify service needs and gaps in care. The Chair requested continued updates to 
clarify the discrepancy between homelessness counts and available  shelter capacity, particularly 
regarding the availability of placements if encampments are removed.
Alex clarified that the previously cited figure of 1,200 represented a county -level count, not 
Worcester alone. He noted that the City’s most recent point-in-time count identified approximately 
60–120 unsheltered individuals, while the total sheltered and unsheltered population was generally 
in the 300s. He emphasized that homelessness fluctuates throughout the year as individuals enter 
and exit the system. 
 
Alex added that the City is focused on maximizing existing resources and connecting individuals 
with appropriate housing, shelter, clinical care, and behavioral health services. Fran requested that 
the Board continue to receive updates. 
 
10. Temporary Protected Status (TPS): The city’s plan and response to community and 
public health impacts associated with the changes.  
The Board requested an update on the City’s response to changes affecting individuals with 
Temporary Protected Status (TPS). Seema reported no significant new data and noted that the 
Mayor, City Manager, and community partners meet approximately every thre e weeks to discuss 
immigration-related concerns and coordinate access to legal assistance, healthcare, food pantries, 
shelters, and other resources. 
Fran asked whether the group also coordinates with hotlines tracking individuals detained by 
federal immigration authorities. Seema explained that discussions address immigration issues 
broadly, with the current focus on connecting individuals navigating immigration proceedings with 
legal assistance and other support to help them understand their status and available options for 
remaining in the country lawfully. 
The chair acknowledged Michael Perotto, a board member who joined the meeting remotely. He 
stated that he had been able to hear the earlier discussion regarding the tobacco violation and 
requested that his attendance and vote be included in the record.  
 
Patrick Lowe made a motion to reconsider the item to allow Michael to participate in the vote. 
All voted in the affirmative with Frances Anthes -yes, Joseph Kahoro -yes and Patrick Lowe – yes. 
 
The Chair confirmed that Michael’s vote would be recorded, resulting in a 4 –0 vote to accept the 
staff recommendation to uphold the tobacco violations as reported. 
 
11. City Council Civilian Review Board Update  
The Chair provided an update on the Board’s prior involvement with the proposed Civilian Review 
Board. The Board reviewed materials from 2021 documenting its unanimous support for the 
creation of a Civilian Review Board with subpoena powers, following a pu blic hearing on 
institutional racism, police reform, and public health. The Board had  also received presentations 
and information regarding the implementation of civilian review boards in other jurisdictions. 
The Chair noted that the Board’s interest in the issue stemmed from concerns regarding the public 
health implications of community violence and safe policing. In August, staff were asked to review
the Board’s prior actions and consult with the City Manager regarding whether the Board of Health 
or Human Rights Commission should have a role moving forward. 
The Chair reported that, following changes including the implementation of police body cameras 
and the release of reports addressing policing in Worcester, the City Manager indicated that the 
issue would be more appropriately addressed by the Human Rights Commission rather than the 
Board of Health. The Chair stated that the Board of Health remains willing to assist the Human 
Rights Commission if needed but that the matter is not currently on the Board’s agenda. 
Patrick thanked the Chair for the historical overview and noted that, although he was not a Board 
member at the time, he recognized the broader public concerns surrounding the issue. He 
emphasized the importance of maintaining a broad public health perspec tive when considering 
policies that affect Worcester residents, including tobacco regulations, policing practices, 
immigration enforcement, and the needs of individuals experiencing homelessness. Patrick stated 
that while the Civilian Review Board matter has since progressed through other City channels, the 
Board should continue to provide a forum for considering the public health implications of 
significant policies and issues affecting the community. Michael thanked Patrick for his comments 
and expressed his support for the perspective presented.  
12.  Adjournment 
The Chair asked for a motion to adjourn, noting that there were no further agenda items or reports.  
13. Next Meeting Date & Topics 
The Board was reminded that the next meeting is scheduled for Monday, October 19, at 6:30 p.m. 
and will be held in person. It was noted that Michael would participate virtually due to travel. 
 
A motion to adjourn was made by Michael Perotto. The motion passed unanimously.  Joseph 
Kahoro -yes, Michael Perotto – yes, Patrick Lowe – yes and Frances Anthes - yes 
 
The meeting adjourned at 7:49p.m.

 Report to the Worcester Board of Health 
 Subject: First State Violation – Sale of Tobacco Product to a Minor 
 Business: Olympic Wine and Spirits, 345 Grafton Street, Worcester, MA 01604 
 Date of Violation: July 24, 2026 
 Hearing Date: September 30, 2026 
Summary of Incident 
On July 24, 2026, the Worcester Division of Public Health (WDPH) conducted a youth 
tobacco compliance check as part of the citywide tobacco enforcement program. During 
this operation, Kyle O’Connor, Public Health Prevention Specialist, directly observed the 
sale of 5 Backwoods White Cigars to a youth, under the age of 21, at Olympic Wine and 
Spirits at 345 Grafton Street, Worcester. 
During the transaction, the clerk did not ask the youth for their ID nor asked their date of 
birth. A receipt was provided after the purchase was made. 
The sale constitutes a violation of Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 270, Section 
6(b), which prohibits the sale of tobacco products to individuals under the age of 21. 
Retailers are required to verify the purchaser’s age through a valid, government-issued 
photographic identification, in accordance with 105 CMR 665.000 – Minimum Standards 
for Retail Sale of Tobacco. 
The business was notified of the violation over the phone the following day and issued a 
$1,000 citation and 3-day tobacco license suspension for this offense, consistent with 
the state and local penalty schedule for a first violation within a 36-month period. 
Violation History 
This is the first violation for this establishment within a 36-month period.
Division of Public Health  
Seema Dixit, Commissioner - Health & Human Services  
Jennifer Bradford, MD, MPH, HHS Medical Director 
Nikki Nixon, MS- DPH Director  
25 Meade Street, Worcester, MA 01610-2715  
P| 508-799-8531 F| 508-799-8572  
health@worcesterma.gov  
 
 
 
Applicable Regulations 
Under Worcester Tobacco Regulations, section H(b), a first violation within 36 months 
results in: 
“a fine of one thousand dollars ($1,000.00) for a State Law violation shall be issued and, if 
the violation is the sale of a tobacco product to a Minor the Tobacco Product Sales Permit 
shall be suspended for three (3) consecutive business days” 
Notice of Hearing 
The retailer was formally notified by phone on September 22, 2026, stating that the 
Worcester Board of Health will hold a public hearing on Wednesday, September 30, 
2026, at 6:30 PM in Room 109 at 25 Meade Street, Worcester. The purpose of this hearing 
is to allow the retailer an opportunity to be heard before the Board votes on the proposed 
suspension. 
Recommendation 
In accordance with 105 CMR 665.000 and the Worcester Tobacco Regulations (revised 
in July 2026), WDPH recommends that the Worcester Board of Health uphold the 
required sanction for a first violation: 
 $1,000 fine (already issued), and 
 3-day suspension of the retailer’s tobacco sales permit. 
This enforcement action is consistent with both state regulations and the City of Worcester 
Tobacco Control Enforcement Policy and aims to promote compliance, protect youth, and 
maintain public health standards across all licensed retailers.

2. Arborviral Activity 
Arboviral diseases 
• Mosquito surveillance indicates active WNV transmission, with 338 positive 
mosquito samples statewide within the 14 counties and 11 recent human 
cases, including one in Worcester County; risk for Worcester County 
remains moderate. Plymouth County has also seen 26 positive EEE 
mosquito samples 
• Recent rainfall and warm daytime temperatures will support increased 
populations of mosquito species capable of spreading WNV and EEE, raising 
seasonal transmission risk until the first cold frost. 
• Prevention measures: 
– Use EPA-approved repellents when outdoors. 
– Wear long sleeves and long pants from dusk to dawn when weather permits. 
– Avoid peak mosquito activity (dusk–dawn). 
– Remove standing water from containers and tarps twice weekly. 
– Use mosquito netting for infants in carriages or playpens. 
• Pet protection: Consult veterinarians about animal-safe repellents and 
recommended vaccinations for WNV and EEE; report suspected animal cases to 
state authorities. 
Check your risk level throughout the season: 
Massachusetts arbovirus update | Mass.gov 
The CDC continues to post multiple travel health notices for mosquito-borne 
diseases. For a complete list of Travel Health notices visit: 
Travel Health Notices | Travelers' Health | CDC
3. Vaccine Corner 
Upcoming vaccination clinics 
• Three days of clinics for preschoolers are scheduled at the three Head Start schools 
on September 28, 29, and 30 from 12 pm to 6 pm at each school. 
• This schedule allows parents to bring their children to our tents after school 
without missing work. 
• Typically, around 100 students are vaccinated for flu across these three schools each 
fall. 
• Per the head nurse we expect to vaccinate 70 students from these 
schools this Fall. Nursing students from Assumption University and 
Worcester State University along with at least one MRC (Medical Reserve 
Corp) volunteer are scheduled to help out. 
 
Final note 
The annual review of the City’s respiratory illness policy for employees is complete and 
being sent to the City Manager’s Office for signature and posting on the City website.

KRATOM: What is Kratom?
WORCESTER DIVISION OF PUBLIC HEALTH | INSPECTIONAL SERVICES
KRATOM
Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is a plant native to Southeast Asia.
There is an increase in concentrated and synthetic 7-7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH)
 Kratom products. They cause more intense opioid-like effects than natural kratom products, and can be highly variable in 
content, concentration, and potency. 
Lower doses may cause stimulant-like effects, such as increased alertness. 
Higher doses may cause opioid-like effects, such as pain relief and sedation.
